To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the optimization of the charge transfer process can be obtained by a combination of solvent engineering and chemical modification of the chromophore(s), which can lead to a 100-fold increase in the rate of electron transfer.

the optimization of the charge-separation step can be achieved by a continuous feedback with synthetic chemists, and that the optimization of this step is crucial for the design of functional multistep systems.

(1) the deactivation dynamics of light-absorbing molecules can be fully disclosed by steady-state and transient spectroscopic methods; (2) by changing the solvent, the deactivation pathway can be optimized; (3) by changing the structure of the chromophore, the deactivation pathways can be optimized; and (4) by changing the components of the multicomponent structure, the deactivation dynamics can be optimized.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the design of functional multilayer structures for light to charge energy conversion, based on the use of a series of prototypical chromophoric systems: polypyridine ruthenium complexes and porphirinoid systems.
the rational design of functional arrays of molecules for light harvesting and conversion into chemical energy.
the design of functional multichromophoric systems, with the aim of achieving light-to-chemical energy conversion, with the ultimate goal of the development of artificial photosynthetic devices.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the design and optimization process of functional multicomponents for charge separation is a complex and challenging task, but it can be performed with a rigorous approach.
the optimization of the light-to-chemical energy conversion efficiency is a multidisciplinary process involving the collaboration between chemists, physicists, and engineers.
a rational design approach for light to chemical conversion is possible, but it is not trivial, and requires the combined efforts of a multidisciplinary research group.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the functional multicomponent systems for charge separation are not a simple sum of the properties of the single components.

we have shown that, by a careful choice of the solvent, it is possible to tune the charge separation yield and kinetics in a large series of chromophore-based multicomponent assemblies, thus opening the way to a rational approach for the optimization of these systems.

the design and optimization process is a continuous feedback between synthesis and photophysical characterization, and that the final structure is the result of a rational design based on the full understanding of the deactivation dynamics of each component.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the design and optimization process of functional structures is a continuous feedback between the experimental and theoretical groups, and it requires a deep knowledge of the photophysical and photochemical processes occurring within the system.

a careful and detailed study of the photophysics of the chromophores, coupled with a rational design of the multicomponent system, is the key for the successful design of functional arrays for light to chemical conversion.
the design of a functional structure is not a matter of luck but can be achieved by a systematic procedure.
